title: Langar where disaster strikes
hook: Sikh volunteers cook free meals after floods, earthquakes and wars around the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, Oak Creek: six worshipers killed, and a sangat that fed strangers the same week. Your line was the doors stayed open. Today, the kitchen behind those doors goes out into the world.

A border crossing in winter. Thousands of families have just walked out of a war zone, carrying what they could. They're cold, and nobody has eaten properly in days. At the edge of the crowd, under a tent, a few people in turbans and orange scarves are stirring enormous pots: rice, dal, hot tea with milk and sugar. Anyone can take a plate. No one asks your name, your religion or your papers. Scenes like this have turned up after floods, earthquakes and wars.
screen: `A BORDER CROSSING IN WINTER.` → `ENORMOUS POTS UNDER A TENT.` → `NO ONE ASKS YOUR NAME.`

segments.voice: Langar has been on this path from the start: the gurdwara's free kitchen, where everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food. At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the kitchen runs all day for whoever comes. Sikhs trace it to Guru Nanak. A janamsakhi story says that when Nanak was a young man, his father gave him money to strike a good bargain, and he spent it all feeding hungry holy men on the road. He called it the true bargain. Guru Angad and his wife, Mata Khivi, built the kitchen into daily life, and tradition says Guru Amar Das asked visitors to eat in the langar before they met him, rich or poor, side by side. Now the langar travels. In 1999, a British Sikh started Khalsa Aid by taking food and supplies to refugees from the war in Kosovo. Since then, Sikh volunteers, from that group and many others, have cooked for flood victims, earthquake survivors, refugees at borders, protesters, and people locked down in the pandemic. In Houston after a hurricane, local Sikhs loaded their cars with hot meals. In their own cities, gurdwaras have fed truck drivers stuck on the highway and neighbors who lost power. Why? Seva, selfless service, and the teaching that the one light is in everyone. The hungry person at a border is not a stranger to be pitied, but a guest at the Guru's table. This week ran from the Komagata Maru, Thind, Britain, the turban in court, September 2001 and Oak Creek to this: langar going out to the world.
screen: `LANGAR: THE GURU'S KITCHEN.` · `THE TRUE BARGAIN.` · `FOOD AT BORDERS, FLOODS, QUAKES.` · `A GUEST AT THE GURU'S TABLE.` · then, large: `THE KITCHEN TRAVELS.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where people are hungry or displaced right now, after a flood, a quake or a war, and picture one family there sitting down to a plate of warm food someone else cooked. Let yourself feel glad for that plate. Then choose one way you could help, however small: a donation, a volunteer hour, a meal for a neighbor.
Langar. The gurdwara's free kitchen — Sikh volunteers carry it to disaster, cooking free meals for anyone after floods, earthquakes and wars around the world.
Your line: the kitchen travels. From Kosovo to Houston, the pots keep stirring. That's day three hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras serve free langar to anyone every day, and Sikh volunteers and aid groups set up kitchens after disasters and at refugee crossings, as seva, selfless service.
